question: Led by Member States like Italy, the EU has been collecting and recycling an extremely high percentage of waste paper in recent years, yet the gradual closure of paper mills is steadily reducing Europe’s capacity to process this waste into finished goods.
As a result, the EU exports large quantities of sorted paper to third countries – India foremost among them – only to then reimport the resulting finished goods, an illogical arrangement.

The loss of domestic production capacity doesn’t just make the European pulp and paper sector less competitive and harm the environment, it also increases Europe's dependence on external markets, a state of affairs that is at odds with the EU’s strategic autonomy and sustainability objectives. In the light of the above: 1.

Will the Commission make use of industrial policy tools, investment incentives, streamlined authorisation procedures, initiatives supporting technological innovation and/or other measures with a view to supporting European paper manufacturing and helping the industry increase its production capacity?

Can the Commission clarify whether and how it will ensure that the implementation of the Union’s circular economy objectives does not give rise to the exportation of secondary raw materials, but rather takes the form of measures bolstering European production chains – an approach that would be in keeping with the principle of industrial sovereignty and the EU’s Green Deal strategies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.3.2026) In January 2025, the Commission presented the Competitiveness Compass1, a new roadmap to restore the EU’s dynamism and boost economic growth.

The European pulp and paper industry benefits from a large range of policies announced in the Competitiveness Compass and already adopted by the Commission such as the EU Omnibus Packages2, the Clean Industrial Deal3 as well as the Action Plan on Affordable Energy4.

In November 2025, the Commission presented the Strategic Framework for a Competitive and Sustainable EU Bioeconomy (EU Bioeconomy Strategy)5, which aims to boost innovation and support European companies in making a success of the green transition. The European pulp and paper industry will benefit from many actions announced in the EU Bioeconomy Strategy such as the creation of lead markets for bio-based materials.

Specifically in respect of the export of waste from the EU, new and stricter waste export rules under the Waste Shipment Regulation6 will ensure that waste is exported only where it can be ensured that it will be managed in conditions that are equivalent to those required in the EU. It is expected that more waste will be retained in the EU as a result of that stricter regime.
